plan.topic: Is Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro? Correcting the myth: same molecule (tirzepatide), different approved uses
plan.angle: Sentence 1: 'Is Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro? Both labels list the same medicine: tirzepatide.' By 6 s: both US prescribing information documents name tirzepatide as the active ingredient. The difference is what each is approved for (each PI's Section 1 indication, copied exactly with its populations) and the trials behind each. One line: 'Side-effect rates differ between the labels because the trial populations differed, so they can't be compared head to head.' One GI line ('mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'). 'Same ingredient doesn't mean interchangeable for you. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' Close with 'Not personal advice', the full prescriber line, then 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' No Exp F line.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide: Is Zepbound Stronger Than Mounjaro? #shorts

plan.why: Spin-off of L1. A myth-busting question that drives viewers to the Mounjaro vs Zepbound long video and covers the 20:00 funnel slot until the holiday series starts on 11-18. | fact-check: A worthwhile myth correction: both US labels list tirzepatide as the active ingredient, and the labels differ in approved uses and trial populations. Sentence 1 as written ('Is tirzepatide as Zepbound stronger than Mounjaro?') is awkward and would make a confusing caption. The indications must be copied from each PI's current Section 1. Mounjaro now includes pediatric T2D (10+) and may include a CV risk-reduction indication, so 'type 2 diabetes in adults' alone would be inaccurate. Don't claim the two brands come in identical strengths or devices. Stick to 'same active ingredient'. Don't call the myth 'false' in a way that implies the two are interchangeable for a given patient. Pair the correction with the don't-switch line. Separate it from L1 by putting the 'stronger?' question at the centre, not the full comparison.

Zepbound isn't the "stronger" version of Mounjaro 👀

Same active ingredient, different jobs:
→ Both US labels list tirzepatide as the active ingredient
→ Mounjaro: blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes (adults and kids 10+), plus lowering major heart-event risk in high-risk adults with type 2 diabetes
→ Zepbound: long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition — and moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity
→ Each label's side effect rates come from different trials in different people, so they can't be compared head to head

Same ingredient doesn't mean interchangeable. Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.

Save this for the next time someone says one is "stronger" than the other.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every claim against the current Zepbound and Mounjaro US Prescribing Information. Both pages load and both show "Revised: 8/2026".
- **Same ingredient (s1–s2):** Both labels name tirzepatide as the active ingredient (Section 11). So "isn't stronger" is fair as a statement about the ingredient.
- **Mounjaro approvals (s3):** Section 1 says "adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years of age and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus". It also covers lowering the risk of major heart events (CV death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk of them.
- **Zepbound approvals (s4):** Section 1 says "reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction long term in adults with obesity or adults with overweight in the presence of at least one weight-related comorbid condition". It also covers moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Both uses are paired with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.
- **Stomach side effects (s6):** The Zepbound label says "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time" in Studies 1 and 2, the weight-reduction trials. The script's "most" and its scope both match.

Safety and closing lines:
- The don't-switch/stop/change line is there. There is no emergency trigger in this script, so the plain scoped line is fine.
- The closing order is right for content dated 2026-11-16 and the 20:00 slot, which has no Exp F card.
- There is no dosing and no talk of compounded products.

Word count: my count is 157 spoken words, not the 154 noted in the cta. That is still within 160, and 159 after the s5 fix below. Nothing is wrong enough to fail. There are three small wording fixes.

issues.claim: Each label's rates come from different trials in different people, so they can't be compared head to head.
issues.problem: Once s5 dropped its setup line, the spoken words no longer say which rates are meant. Only the card says 'side effect'. Someone just listening hears 'rates' straight after the approvals list and may think it means weight-loss or approval rates.
issues.fix: Each label's side effect rates come from different trials in different people, so they can't be compared head to head. (Adds 2 words, bringing the total to 159, still within 160.)

issues.claim: List ends with 'Alongside diet and exercise' after the major-heart-event item
issues.problem: The Mounjaro label pairs 'adjunct to diet and exercise' only with blood sugar control, not with the heart-event approval. Putting it last makes it look as if it covers both uses.
issues.fix: Replace the items with: ["Mounjaro (US label)", "Blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes, alongside diet and exercise", "Adults and children 10 and older", "Lower risk of major heart events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high heart risk"]

issues.claim: Zepbound: weight reduction in adults with obesity...
issues.problem: The card leaves out 'long-term', which the narration and the label ('maintain weight reduction long term') both include. The card ends up saying less than the narration.
issues.fix: Zepbound: long-term weight reduction in adults with obesity, or overweight + 1 weight-related condition. Moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity.
